title: Connection Pooling with PgBouncer
description: Architect scalable PostgreSQL connection pooling using PgBouncer, handle transaction mode limitations, and configure connection limits.

data.text: PostgreSQL forks a separate operating system process for every connected client. Because each process consumes 5-10MB of RAM, connecting hundreds of serverless function instances directly to PostgreSQL will crash the database server. **PgBouncer** is a lightweight connection pooler that maintains a small pool of persistent database connections and reuses them across thousands of client requests.

When connecting Prisma to PgBouncer in transaction mode (the standard mode in Supabase, AWS RDS, and Neon), you must append `?pgbouncer=true` to your connection string. This tells Prisma Client's query engine to disable PostgreSQL prepared statements, which are incompatible with transaction-level pooling across multiple connections.

data.title: schema.prisma with Dual URLs for PgBouncer
data.content: Configuring url for runtime pooling and directUrl for migrations.

data.title: .env Connection Strings
data.content: Setting connection parameters in your environment configuration.
data.code:
# Pooled connection for Next.js App (PgBouncer port 6543)
DATABASE_URL="postgres://user:pass@ep-pooler.region.neon.tech:6543/db?pgbouncer=true&connection_limit=10"

# Direct connection for Prisma Migrate (Direct port 5432)
DIRECT_URL="postgres://user:pass@ep-direct.region.neon.tech:5432/db"

data.title: The `connection_limit` Parameter
data.text: In serverless environments, set `connection_limit=1` or `connection_limit=5` in your connection string so that individual serverless lambdas do not hoard pooler slots.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: PgBouncer multiplexes thousands of incoming client requests over a small set of database connections.
Always append `?pgbouncer=true` when using transaction mode to disable prepared statements.
Use `directUrl` for migrations because advisory locks require direct session access.
